title: The Last Day: raised and weighed
hook: the resurrection, the reckoning, the garden and the fire
carry: an atom's weight of good will be seen

segments.voice: Yesterday, rusul, the messengers, and your line: every people had one. Named or unnamed, every nation was sent someone.

Tradition says a man in Mecca picked up an old bone, crumbled it in his hand, and asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ a mocking question. Who's going to bring this back to life once it's rotted away? The Qur'an records the question, and the answer that comes back is very short: the one who made it the first time will make it again. That exchange sits near the end of Surah Ya Sin, and tradition links that surah with the dying and the dead.
screen: `A CRUMBLING BONE.` → `WHO BRINGS THIS BACK?` → `THE ONE WHO MADE IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: The word for it is akhirah, the hereafter, the life that comes last. The Qur'an keeps setting it beside dunya, this near world, the one we're in now. Belief in the Last Day has four movements. First, the resurrection. The bodies of the dead are raised, the bone in the man's hand included. The answer in Ya Sin argues from the first creation: making something again is no harder than making it at all. Second, the reckoning. Every life is laid open. Surah az-Zalzalah, a short surah about the earth shaking, ends with two lines: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, And whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then." Nothing is too small to count, in either direction. Third, the two homes. The Qur'an describes a garden, with rivers, shade and peace, and a fire. It describes both vividly, and hides neither. Fourth, the One behind it. In the opening surah, al-Fatiha, Allah is called the Merciful and the master of the Day of Judgment in the same breath. Mercy and reckoning sit side by side. And this is why the Last Day sits among the six. For Muslims, it gives the ordinary day its weight: the kind word, the shortcut not taken, the atom of good nobody else saw.
screen: `THE BONES ARE RAISED.` · `AN ATOM'S WEIGHT.` · `A GARDEN AND A FIRE.` · then, large: `MERCIFUL, AND MASTER OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Think of meeting Him, or, if that isn't your language, of your life being seen whole. Bring up one small good thing from this week, a door held, a message answered kindly, and let it be seen; then one small harm, and let that be seen too, without arguing. If you pray, you can recite the opening surah slowly, with its two names, the Merciful and master of the Day; if not, just rest in being seen.
Akhirah. The hereafter, the life that comes last: the resurrection, the reckoning, the garden and the fire. The fifth article of faith. Today's word.
Your line: an atom's weight of good will be seen. Tomorrow, the sixth and final article of faith: the decree. Peace to you.

howItsDone: Belief in the Last Day is the fifth article of faith; Muslims recite al-Fatiha, which names Allah as master of the Day of Judgment, in prayer, and Surah Ya Sin may be read for the dying and the dead.

chat.says: Does Islam say small things count, or only big sins and big good deeds?
options: Small things count. Az-Zalzalah says even an atom's weight of good or ill is seen.
Only the big things. Small deeds are too slight to weigh on the Last Day.
Only what others saw counts; deeds done in private aren't recorded.
